title: Press on (Philippians 3:12–21)
hookLine: forgetting what lies behind, straining forward

cards: Watch the last fifty meters of a race. Nobody in the lead looks back. Coaches drill it: turn your head to see who's behind you, and you lose a step.
The runners lean forward, chest out, reaching for a line on the ground. Paul has just told the Philippians that everything behind him is loss.
Now he faces the other way, and reaches for the language of the stadium: a track, a line, a prize.

teach.b: He starts with an admission. Paul, the great apostle, says he hasn't arrived. In the King James Bible: "Brethren, I count not myself to have apprehended."
Not yet. I haven't got hold of it.

Then the well-known lines: "this one thing I do, forgetting those things which are behind, and reaching forth unto those things which are before, I press toward the mark for the prize of the high calling of God in Christ Jesus."
Every phrase is a runner. Forgetting what's behind. Reaching forth, the body leaning out.
The mark, the goal at the end of the track. The prize. The verb for press is worth a second look.
In Greek it's a word for chasing, pursuing hard.

A few verses earlier, Paul used the very same word about his past: he had been zealous, persecuting the church. The same energy that once hunted Christians now runs toward Christ. Paul doesn't become a calmer man.
He points the same drive in a new direction. And forgetting isn't amnesia. He remembers his past well enough to write it down a few verses earlier.
He means it no longer steers: not his old credentials, not his old wrongs. Then he widens the picture: "For our conversation is in heaven."
You live here, he says, but your city is somewhere else.

how: Some Christians turn to Philippians 3:13–14 at new beginnings, such as a new year, a graduation or a recovery.

o: chase hard toward a goal, like a runner
keep quiet and endure whatever comes
push through pain until you finally collapse

games.q: what's inside Philippians 3:12–21 — tap the pairs.
p: I count not myself to have apprehended
the goal at the end of the track
of the high calling of God

s: Paul says he has already reached perfection
he says plainly he hasn't got hold of it yet. that's why he keeps running.
forgetting what's behind means Paul erased his past
he had just written his past down. he means it no longer steers.
Paul uses the same Greek verb for pressing on that he used for persecuting the church
in 3:6 he was persecuting the church; in 3:14 he presses toward the mark.

games.q: you're running the last stretch of a race and you hear footsteps behind you. what do you do?
o: look back to see who it is.
forget what's behind and reach for the line.
slow down and let them pass.
games.why: Paul's picture: "forgetting those things which are behind, and reaching forth unto those things which are before."

practice: Think of something you keep replaying, a failure, an old win, a conversation you can't stop rewriting, and notice how much attention it still takes.
Then gently turn your head the other way: what's one small thing in front of you that you've put off while you looked back, a call, a page, an apology, a first lap?
Picture taking the first step toward it, just one, and if you pray, ask for help to run.

wordCard.voice: Press on. Paul's runner's word: chase hard toward the goal, the same verb he once used for persecuting, now aimed forward.

orig.note: Greek: to chase, pursue, press on. Paul uses the same verb for persecuting the church in Philippians 3:6.

carryVoice: Your line: forgetting what's behind, reaching forth. The race isn't over yet. See you on the track tomorrow.
